title: Coding-Decoding
shortDescription: Find the ONE consistent shift or substitution rule from the given example, then apply it letter-by-letter or digit-by-digit to the new word.
genZNote: It's not a secret code, it's a pattern with trust issues. Find the shift once, apply it everywhere — the code never changes mid-question.

sections.heading: Core Idea
sections.body: Coding-decoding questions give an example pairing (a word coded into letters/numbers) and ask you to apply the SAME rule to a new word. The method: compare each letter/digit position between the original and the coded version to find the consistent transformation (a fixed alphabetical shift, a reversal, a substitution table), then apply that exact rule — not a guessed variation — to the new input.

sections.heading: Common Rule Types
bullets: Fixed alphabetical shift: every letter moves forward or backward by the same fixed number of positions (e.g. A→D, B→E is a +3 shift).
Reversal: the letters of the word are coded in reverse order, sometimes combined with a shift.
Position-based substitution: each letter is replaced by its numeric position in the alphabet (A=1, B=2, ...), sometimes with an added/subtracted constant.
Symbol/number substitution table: each letter maps to a specific symbol or digit given directly in the question, with no arithmetic pattern — just read the table.

steps.name: Find the rule from the example
steps.explanation: If CAT is coded as DBU, compare position by position: C→D (+1), A→B (+1), T→U (+1). The rule is a uniform +1 alphabetical shift.
steps.purpose: Confirm the SAME shift applies to every letter before trusting the rule — a rule that only fits one letter isn't the real rule.

steps.name: Apply it to the new word
steps.explanation: Code DOG using the same +1 shift: D→E, O→P, G→H. DOG codes to EPH.
steps.purpose: Mechanical application of the confirmed rule — no re-guessing needed.

sections.heading: Common Traps
bullets: Assuming a shift found for one or two letters applies to the whole word without checking every letter — a rule must hold consistently across ALL letters of the example.
Forgetting to wrap around the alphabet (after Z comes A again) for a shift that would otherwise run past Z.
Missing a reversal combined with a shift — always check if the coded letters are also in reverse order of the original word.

sections.heading: Exam Strategy
bullets: Write the original word and its code directly above/below each other, letter aligned with letter, before looking for the pattern — this makes a shift or reversal visually obvious.
Verify the rule against every letter in the given example before applying it to the new word; a rule confirmed on only 1 of 3 letters is not yet confirmed.

quickRevision.oneLineDefinition: Coding-decoding finds one consistent letter/digit transformation rule from a given example and applies it unchanged to a new word.
keyFacts: Common rule types: fixed alphabetical shift, reversal, position-number substitution, or a given symbol table.
A shift must be verified across every letter of the example before being trusted.
Alphabet shifts wrap around after Z back to A.
commonConfusion: A pattern that fits only part of the example word is not yet a confirmed rule — check every letter.

highYieldFacts: Aligning the original and coded word letter-by-letter makes the transformation rule visually obvious.
commonTraps: Trusting a shift confirmed on only part of the example word.
mustRemember: Confirm the rule against every letter of the given example before applying it to a new word.
